opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the early struggles came from the fact that I started out as a researcher, not as a manager. When you're doing a PhD, your job is basically to go deep on a problem, write the code yourself, and stay up all night until something works. That mindset got Taichi started, but it doesn't scale when you suddenly have a team, investors, and users depending on you.

In the beginning I kept trying to solve everything personally. If there was a hard bug, I wanted to fix it. If there was a design decision, I wanted to make it. And that felt productive, but really I was becoming the bottleneck. It took me a while to realize that as a CEO, my output isn't the code I write; it's the decisions the team can make without me, and the clarity of direction I give them.

The other thing was learning that a technically elegant product isn't automatically a business. In academia, if the idea is beautiful and the paper is strong, people pay attention. In a company, you have to ask: who actually needs this, what problem does it solve for them today, and will they pay for it? I underestimated how different those two worlds are, and I made some mistakes because of that.

So the way I make sense of it now is that those struggles were tuition. Painful, sometimes embarrassing, but necessary. I don't think I could have learned those lessons by reading books. I had to make the mistakes, feel the consequences, and then adjust. And I'm still learning. I don't think anyone ever fully "graduates" from being a founder.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, when I look back at those early days, the biggest struggle wasn't technical at all, and that surprised me. I came out of a PhD at MIT where I'd spent years building Taichi as a research project. I knew how to write a compiler. I knew how to make GPU code run fast. What I didn't know was how to run a company, and there was no paper I could read to fix that.

The first thing I had to make sense of was the gap between being a good researcher and being a good CEO. In research, you optimize for being right and for being novel. As a CEO, you optimize for the team moving in the same direction, even when you're not sure you're right. Those are almost opposite instincts. Early on I would spend days perfecting some design decision that, in hindsight, didn't matter nearly as much as hiring the right second engineer or talking to one more user.

The second struggle was figuring out what we were actually building. Taichi started as a programming language for graphics and simulation, and it had a passionate open-source community. But a language is not a product, and a community is not a customer base. We had to learn where the real pain was, which turned out to be much more about making high-performance computing accessible to people who weren't CUDA experts than about any particular feature of the language. That took a lot of uncomfortable conversations and a few pivots in emphasis that I resisted longer than I should have.

And the third thing, which I think is the most personal one, is that I had to accept that struggling was the normal state, not a sign I was failing. In academia, you can go a long time without anyone telling you that you're wrong. As a founder, you get told you're wrong constantly, by the market, by investors, sometimes by your own team. I had to learn to separate "this hurts" from "this is a problem." A lot of it just hurt and wasn't a problem.

So how do I make sense of it? I think of those early years as the period when I was learning a second profession while trying to practice it at the same time. It was inefficient and often humbling. But I don't think there's a shortcut. The open-source background actually helped more than I expected, because open source teaches you to listen to people who owe you nothing, and that's exactly the skill a founder needs.

astra-6.text:
I think of those early struggles as a transition from solving technical problems to learning how to build a company. As an engineer, you’re used to making progress by understanding a problem deeply and working on it yourself. As a CEO, that isn’t enough. You need to decide which problems matter, communicate why they matter, and help other people succeed at solving them.

That shift can be uncomfortable because the skills that made you confident in one role don’t automatically carry over to the next. But I don’t think struggling necessarily means you’re the wrong person for the job. It means you have things to learn. The important part is being honest about what isn’t working and being willing to change how you work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest part was learning that being a founder and CEO is a different job from being a researcher or engineer. When you’re technical, you’re used to making progress by solving a problem yourself. As a CEO, you have to help other people succeed, decide what matters most, and make decisions with incomplete information.

I’m still learning that. I try to look at those early struggles as feedback: What did I misunderstand? What should I have communicated more clearly? What do I need to change? That makes them useful, even when they’re uncomfortable.
